items.stem: In a floating exchange rate system, the exchange rate is determined by
options: the central bank setting a fixed rate
the demand for and supply of the currency
items.answer: the demand for and supply of the currency
items.markingKey: No official intervention to target a rate.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how an increase in demand for a country’s exports affects a floating exchange rate.
items.answer: Diagram: price of currency (in foreign currency) on vertical axis, quantity of currency horizontal. Foreigners need more of the currency to pay for exports, so demand shifts right and the exchange rate appreciates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diagram; 1 mark: demand shifts right; 1 mark: appreciation [3]

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of a fixed exchange rate system.
items.answer: Loss of independent monetary policy; need for large reserves; risk of speculative attack; misalignment causing deficits or unemployment; no automatic BoP adjustment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Speculators expect Sundara’s fixed exchange rate to be devalued and sell its currency heavily. Analyse the options available to the central bank and their consequences.
items.answer: Buy the currency with reserves (reserves may run out); raise interest rates to attract inflows (harms growth and employment); impose capital controls; or devalue/float (loss of credibility, imported inflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each option analysed (up to 3); 1 mark judgement [4]

items.stem: Speculators expect Dravonia’s fixed exchange rate to be devalued and sell its currency heavily. Analyse the options available to the central bank and their consequences.
items.answer: Buy the currency with reserves (reserves may run out); raise interest rates to attract inflows (harms growth and employment); impose capital controls; or devalue/float (loss of credibility, imported inflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each option analysed (up to 3); 1 mark judgement [4]

items.stem: Extract: Sundara abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 4 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 5 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Calculate the percentage depreciation of the currency against the dollar. (b) Explain why reserves fell under the fixed rate.
items.answer: (a) 20% (the dollar has appreciated by 25%) (b) The central bank sold dollars to buy its currency to defend the peg against excess supply/speculation.

items.stem: To maintain a fixed exchange rate when the currency is under downward pressure, the central bank can
options: buy its own currency using foreign exchange reserves
items.answer: buy its own currency using foreign exchange reserves
items.markingKey: Or raise interest rates.

items.stem: Tourism to Nordavia increases sharply. Explain, using demand and supply, the effect on its floating exchange rate.
items.answer: Tourists must buy the currency to spend in Nordavia, so demand for the currency shifts right and the exchange rate appreciates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: demand shift; 1 mark: appreciation [2]

items.stem: Tourism to Istrana increases sharply. Explain, using demand and supply, the effect on its floating exchange rate.
items.answer: Tourists must buy the currency to spend in Istrana, so demand for the currency shifts right and the exchange rate appreciates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: demand shift; 1 mark: appreciation [2]

items.stem: Tourism to Umbria Nova increases sharply. Explain, using demand and supply, the effect on its floating exchange rate.
items.answer: Tourists must buy the currency to spend in Umbria Nova, so demand for the currency shifts right and the exchange rate appreciates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: demand shift; 1 mark: appreciation [2]

items.stem: Interest rates in Marvona rise relative to those in Tarvia. Analyse the likely effect on Marvona’s floating exchange rate and its exports.
items.answer: Higher rates attract financial inflows (hot money), raising demand for the currency: appreciation. Exports become dearer in foreign currency and imports cheaper, so export volumes may fall, depending on PED.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capital inflows; 1 mark: appreciation; 1 mark: effect on exports; 1 mark: elasticity caveat [4]

items.stem: Speculators expect Quentara’s fixed exchange rate to be devalued and sell its currency heavily. Analyse the options available to the central bank and their consequences.
items.answer: Buy the currency with reserves (reserves may run out); raise interest rates to attract inflows (harms growth and employment); impose capital controls; or devalue/float (loss of credibility, imported inflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each option analysed (up to 3); 1 mark judgement [4]

items.stem: Halvoria is debating whether to peg its currency to the US dollar. Discuss whether a floating exchange rate is always better than a fixed exchange rate.
items.answer: Arguments for: Automatic BoP adjustment, monetary independence, no reserves needed. Arguments against / evaluation: Volatility and uncertainty for trade and investment, speculation, imported inflation; fixed rates provide discipline; managed float as compromise. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: The real exchange rate adjusts the nominal exchange rate for
options: differences in price levels between countries
items.answer: differences in price levels between countries
items.markingKey: Real = nominal × (domestic price index / foreign price index).

items.stem: Explain why the real exchange rate is a better measure of competitiveness than the nominal exchange rate.
items.answer: It accounts for relative inflation: even if the nominal rate is constant, higher domestic inflation makes exports dearer, so competitiveness depends on both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflation adjustment; 1 mark: link to competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Explain why a trade-weighted index is more useful than a single bilateral exchange rate.
items.answer: A country trades with many partners; the TWI shows the overall change in the currency’s value, weighted by the importance of each partner in trade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: many partners; 1 mark: weighted [2]

items.stem: Kestria’s nominal exchange rate changes by +0% against its main partner. Domestic prices rise by 6% and foreign prices by 1%. Calculate the approximate percentage change in the real exchange rate.

Merania trades with three partners with trade weights of 50%, 30% and 20%. Over a year its currency changes by +8%, -6% and -2% against partners A, B and C. (a) Calculate the trade-weighted index (start = 100). (b) Domestic prices rose 4% and partners’ prices 1% on average. Calculate the change in the real effective exchange rate and explain what it means for competitiveness.
items.answer: (a) TWI = 101.8 (b) real ≈ 101.8 × 104/101 = 104.82, a 4.82% change: a real appreciation, so competitiveness worsens.
items.markingKey: (a) Σ weight × index [2]; (b) adjust by relative prices [2]; interpretation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Istrana abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 8 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 10 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Calculate the percentage depreciation of the currency against the dollar. (b) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) 20% (the dollar has appreciated by 25%) (b) Import prices rise in domestic currency; export demand adds to AD.

items.stem: Marvona’s nominal exchange rate against the dollar has not changed for three years, but its inflation has been 6% a year compared with 2% in the USA. Explain what has happened to its real exchange rate.
items.answer: Domestic prices rose faster than US prices, so the real exchange rate appreciated by roughly 4% a year: its goods became less competitive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: real appreciation; 1 mark: reason/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Halvoria’s nominal exchange rate changes by -5% against its main partner. Domestic prices rise by 4% and foreign prices by 3%. Calculate the approximate percentage change in the real exchange rate.

The exchange rate between the Nordavia krona (K) and the US dollar is $1 = K2. A Nordavia product sells for K400 at home. The exchange rate changes to $1 = K2.4. Calculate the dollar price before and after, state whether the krona has appreciated or depreciated, and explain the likely effect on export revenue.
items.answer: Before $200; after $166.67. The krona depreciates by 16.7%. Dollar price falls, so export volumes rise; revenue in krona rises if demand is elastic.
items.markingKey: Price conversion each rate [2]; correct appreciation/depreciation [1]; PED-based effect on revenue [1].

items.stem: Zentara’s currency has been stable against the dollar but inflation is much higher than in its trading partners. Discuss whether changes in the real exchange rate are more important than changes in the nominal exchange rate.
items.answer: Arguments for: Real rate measures competitiveness. Arguments against / evaluation: Nominal rates affect debt servicing, capital flows and import prices immediately; both needed. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Extract: Rovania abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 8 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 10 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Explain why reserves fell under the fixed rate. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the floating rate was determined.
items.answer: (a) The central bank sold dollars to buy its currency to defend the peg against excess supply/speculation. (b) Demand and supply of the currency; excess supply at the old peg; new lower equilibrium.

items.stem: Purchasing power parity theory states that, in the long run, exchange rates adjust so that
options: identical goods cost the same in different countries when prices are converted into a common currency
interest rates are equal in all countries
all countries have the same GDP
items.answer: identical goods cost the same in different countries when prices are converted into a common currency
items.markingKey: Law of one price applied to baskets.

items.stem: If a burger costs $5 in the USA and 20 units in Country X, the PPP exchange rate is
items.answer: $1 = 4 units of X’s currency

items.stem: Explain two reasons why exchange rates may not move to purchasing power parity.
items.answer: Non-traded goods and services; transport costs and tariffs; capital flows and speculation dominate currency markets; product differentiation; government intervention.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: A basket of groceries costs $4 in the USA and 40 units of local currency in Loristan. Calculate the implied PPP exchange rate.
items.answer: $1 = 10 units

items.stem: A newspaper claims that Jovania’s currency is 30% undervalued. ‘Purchasing power parity theory explains movements in exchange rates.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: Arguments for: Long-run tendency for inflation differentials to be offset by exchange rate changes. Arguments against / evaluation: Short-run dominated by capital flows, interest rates and speculation; non-traded goods; transport costs; useful for comparing living standards. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: A burger costs $6 in the USA and 120 units in Jovania. The market exchange rate is $1 = 30 units. Calculate the implied PPP rate, the dollar price of the burger in Jovania, and the percentage by which Jovania’s currency is over- or undervalued. Explain one limitation of this method.
items.answer: PPP rate $1 = 20; dollar price $4; currency undervalued by 33.3%. Limitation: one product; includes non-traded inputs (rent, wages), taxes and tastes differ.
items.markingKey: PPP = local/US price [1]; dollar price = local/market rate [1]; (dollar price − US price)/US price [2]; limitation [1].
